title: Arrays, readonly tuples, object types, optional and readonly properties
summary: Arrays, tuples and object types describe data; readonly and ? describe what may change and what may be missing. Both are compile-time only and shallow, so know when Object.freeze or a copy is the real guarantee.

examples.title: readonly arrays, tuples and the in-place sort bug

annotations.note: sort() (like reverse() and splice()) mutates the array it is called on, so the caller's data changes behind its back. In Go a slice parameter shares its backing array in the same way.

readonly number[] (also written ReadonlyArray<number>) is the same runtime array with the mutating methods removed from its type. toSorted (ES2023, needs lib es2023+; this app's own tsconfig.app.json uses ES2020 libs, where you'd write [...scores].sort()) returns a sorted copy.
A tuple type fixes length and per-position types; readonly forbids writes. The labels lat and lon are documentation only: they don't change compatibility and destructuring can use any names.
Object.entries yields [key, value] tuples, and destructuring in the callback parameter unpacks them. This is TS's answer to Go's multiple return values.

examples.title: Optional and readonly properties, and their limits

annotations.note: `minutes?: number` means the key may be absent, so every read is number | undefined and the caller picks a default. Unlike Go, there is no zero value: a missing number is undefined, not 0.
readonly applies to the property, not to the value in it. The tags reference can't be replaced, but the array can be pushed to. Use readonly string[] as well when the contents must not change either.
A known hole: readonly properties are ignored when checking assignability, so a mutable type can alias the same object. Readonly arrays are stricter: readonly T[] is not assignable to T[] (TS4104).

Object.freeze is the runtime guarantee, and its return type is Readonly<T>. In strict-mode code (every ES module) a write throws a TypeError; in sloppy scripts it is silently ignored. It is shallow as well: nested arrays and objects stay mutable.

use_cases: readonly T[] parameters on every function that only reads an array, so callers know their data is safe
Readonly tuples for fixed pairs: coordinates, [key, value], a hook's [value, setValue]
Optional properties for genuinely absent data (no estimate yet), not as a way to avoid modelling states
Object.freeze for module-level constants and configuration that must not change at run time
strengths: Unlike Java's unmodifiable views (which throw at run time), readonly arrays remove the mutators from the type, so the mistake is a compile error
Tuples give fixed-length, per-position types without a class, which Java needs a record for and Go a struct or multiple returns
Optional properties make absence part of the type, so a missing field is handled where it is read, not discovered as null later
weaknesses: readonly is shallow and compile-time only; deep immutability needs Readonly types at every level, as const, or a freeze at run time
readonly properties are not enforced on assignment to a mutable type, so an alias can write to them
Arrays and objects are reference types with no copy-on-assign, unlike Go structs; sharing is the default and copying is explicit

pitfalls.title: Mutating an array you were handed
pitfalls.detail: sort, reverse and splice change the caller's array. Use toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced (ES2023) or copy first, and type read-only parameters as readonly T[].
pitfalls.bad: function top(xs: number[]) { return xs.sort((a, b) => b - a)[0]; }
pitfalls.good: function top(xs: readonly number[]) { return xs.toSorted((a, b) => b - a)[0]; }

pitfalls.title: Treating readonly as immutability
pitfalls.detail: readonly stops assignments through that type only. Nested values remain mutable, and another alias without readonly can still write.

pitfalls.title: Optional property where a union of states belongs
pitfalls.detail: `{ data?: T; error?: string }` allows both or neither. If exactly one must be present, use a discriminated union (lesson ts.narrowing.discriminated-unions).

quiz.q: A function takes `xs: readonly string[]`. Can you pass it a `string[]`?
quiz.why: A mutable array can always be viewed read-only. The reverse, readonly string[] to string[], is a compile error (TS4104).

quiz.q: `interface C { readonly tags: string[] }`. Which statement compiles?
quiz.why: readonly protects the property binding, not the array it points to. Make it readonly string[] to block push too.

quiz.q: What does Object.freeze give you that a readonly type does not?
options: Enforcement at run time, one level deep
quiz.why: freeze makes the object's own properties non-writable at run time; nested objects are not frozen.

quiz.q: In `type LatLon = readonly [lat: number, lon: number]`, what do the labels change?
options: They turn the tuple into an object with lat and lon
They make the tuple incompatible with [number, number]
quiz.why: Tuple labels are documentation: the type is still a two-element array of numbers.

further_reading.title: TypeScript Handbook: Object Types (optional, readonly, tuples)

body:
## Concept

Four building blocks cover most data you will type:

- **Arrays**: `string[]` (or `Array<string>`), and `readonly string[]`
  (`ReadonlyArray<string>`), which has no `push`, `sort` or other mutating methods.
- **Tuples**: arrays with a fixed length and a type per position, `[string, number]`,
  optionally labelled and readonly: `readonly [lat: number, lon: number]`.
- **Object types**: inline `{ id: string; title: string }`, or named with `interface`
  or `type`. `Record<string, T>` (or an index signature `{ [key: string]: T }`) types
  dictionaries; with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` their reads include `undefined`.
- **Property modifiers**: `?` marks a property that may be absent, `readonly` one that
  can't be assigned through this type.

`readonly` and `?` are checker-only, like every type. At run time an array is an array
and an object is an object; `Object.freeze` is the only built-in runtime enforcement.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C++: `readonly T[]` is closest to `const std::vector<T>&`: the callee can read but not
  modify. Like C++ `const` it is shallow for pointers inside, and it is weaker: a
  `readonly` property can be aliased as writable without any cast (example 2).
- Java: `final` fields ≈ `readonly` properties; `List.copyOf`/unmodifiable views ≈
  `readonly T[]`, except Java enforces at run time with an exception and TS at compile
  time with a missing method. Records ≈ readonly object types.
- Go: slices share their backing array just as JS arrays are shared references, but Go
  structs are copied on assignment; JS objects never are. There is no zero value: an
  absent optional property reads as `undefined`.
- Python: tuples are immutable at run time; TS tuples are ordinary arrays with a fixed
  type. `typing.Final` and frozen dataclasses are the nearest relatives of `readonly`
  and `Object.freeze`.
- JS: nothing changes at run time. `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` and `with`
  (ES2023) are the copying versions of the mutating array methods.

## Design notes

Make read-only the default in signatures: a function that only reads an array or object
should say so with `readonly T[]` or `Readonly<T>`, which costs nothing and documents
the contract at every call site. Return fresh values rather than mutating inputs (the
copying ES2023 methods and spread make that cheap to write). Reserve `?` for data that
can legitimately be absent; when fields come and go together, model the states as a
discriminated union instead. Reach for `Object.freeze` when something outside the type
system (another module, a library, the console) could write to a shared value.
